newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan assembly enacts constitutional reforms.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan assembly enacts constitutional reforms.

text.p: Taiwan's constitutional congress on Friday adopted amendments to junk the largely redundant provincial government and to beef up the president's powers at the expense of parliament.
"The third and final reading has been completed," state television said after the reforms were adopted in the National Assembly, whose sole function is amending the constitution.

Deep differences between the ruling Nationalist Party and the independence-minded Democratic Progressive Party forced postponement until 1998 of a potentially explosive proposal to give Taiwan's people the right of plebiscite.

The Nationalists have resisted an opposition push to legalise popular referendums, which scholars warn could undermine an uneasy status quo between Taiwan and communist China, ideological rivals since their 1949 civil war split.

The amendments will marginalise the provincial government, a move that will save T$60 billion (US$2.2 billion) a year but which could kindle Beijing's suspicions that Taiwan is moving toward independence rather than eventual reunion with China.

The amendments bolster the power of Taiwan's elected president by stripping the elected parliament of the right to veto the president's choice of cabinet chief and granting the president a new power to dissolve parliament.

Conversely, the amendments give parliament the power to recall the president, but set a very high standard -- requiring a three-fifths vote of the full membership to impeach the chief executive and a two-thirds vote to sack him.
